entries.narration: Before typing anything, it helps to know what you are typing into. Strictly speaking, Linux is one program: the kernel. It is the only software that talks to the hardware directly, and it decides which process runs next, how much memory each one gets, and which files each one is allowed to open. Everything else runs above it, in what is called user space. Your shell, the ls command, the web server, the package manager: all of them are ordinary programs that ask the kernel to do things on their behalf. A distribution, such as Debian thirteen, codenamed trixie, is a set of decisions about that user space. Which packages exist, which versions, which configuration files and defaults, and how updates arrive. Debian also ships a kernel build, but that does not make the kernel and the distribution the same thing, and the two commands at the top of the scene show why. uname dash r asks the running kernel for its release, here six point twelve, built by Debian for trixie. Reading slash etc slash os-release reads a plain file that the distribution installed, and it names Debian thirteen. Most of the time those two agree. Later in this chapter you will see a container where they don't: the kernel belongs to one system, and the files belong to another. Keeping these two identities apart is the first habit of this course. Next, how a powered-off machine becomes a system you can log in to.

When you sit down at a running Linux system, you are seeing the last link in a chain. It is worth knowing the links now, because every boot problem later in the course is found by asking which link broke. Power comes on and the firmware, on modern machines UEFI, looks for a boot loader. On Debian that is usually GRUB, and its whole job is to load two files into memory: the kernel, and a small starter filesystem called the initramfs. The kernel takes over the hardware, and the initramfs does the awkward work of finding the real root filesystem, which might sit on an encrypted disk or a RAID set, and mounting it. Then the kernel starts the very first process, process ID one. On Debian that is systemd. Every other process on the system descends from it. systemd starts services in dependency order until it reaches a goal it calls a target, and one of those services offers a way to log in, whether that is a text console, an SSH server, or a graphical login screen. Once you are authenticated, a shell starts, running as you. That shell is your session. The code card shows systemd-analyze, which breaks the boot into exactly these stages and times each one. Notice that it is a systemd tool, not a portable one. In chapter six we come back to every stage in depth. For now, keep the order. Next: what actually happens between your keyboard and that shell.

Three different programs cooperate every time you run a command, and it pays to be able to name them. The terminal is the window, or the text console, that shows characters and sends your key presses. It does not understand commands at all. The shell does. On Debian, the interactive shell is Bash. It reads the line you typed, splits it into words, works out what the first word refers to, and then runs it. Some commands are built into Bash. Others are separate program files. For ls, Bash creates a child process, the fork, and that child replaces itself with the program at slash usr slash bin slash ls, the exec. ls then asks the kernel to read the directory through system calls, and its output travels back to the terminal. The type command tells you which kind of command a name is. type cd says shell builtin. type ls says it is an alias, a shortcut Debian's default configuration adds for colour, and type dash capital P shows the program file behind it. Here is why the difference matters. Every process has its own current directory. If cd were a separate program, it would change its own directory and then exit, and your shell would be exactly where it was. A child cannot change its parent. So cd has to run inside the shell. Graphical applications follow the same rules: they are processes too, they just draw windows. Next, your first session, read as evidence.

Let's read a first session as evidence. Every line here answers a question, and the habit of asking them before changing anything will save you a lot of confusion later. The first command is id. It shows your user ID, one thousand, your primary group, and the other groups you belong to. Notice that learner is in brackets. The kernel never checks names; it checks numbers, and the name is a label mapped onto the number. That distinction comes back in chapter four. Next, echo dollar HOME prints your home directory. It is set when you log in, from your account record, and the tilde character is shorthand for it. Then pwd, print working directory, shows where this shell currently is. Right after login, home and the current directory are the same place, which is why beginners often confuse them. They are different things. Home is fixed for your account. The current directory belongs to this one shell process, and it is what every relative name is resolved from. The next line creates the course's lab directory. mkdir dash p makes every missing level, and the double ampersand runs cd only if mkdir succeeded. Now pwd reports a different answer, while home has not moved. The box at the bottom shows why that matters. The name incoming, with no leading slash, is resolved from the current directory. From the lab directory, ls incoming finds it. From home, the very same command reports no such file. Nothing about the file changed; only where the shell was standing. Everything in this course happens under tilde slash lab slash reportd, a small project that will grow from a folder of records into a running service. Next: how to read a command line, and where to find its help.

Nobody memorises every option of every command, and you shouldn't try. What you need instead is to read a command line, and to know where its documentation lives. Look at the annotated line in the middle of the scene. ls is the command. Dash l is a short option, one dash and one letter. Dash dash sort equals time is a long option with a value, and long options are a GNU convention you will see across Debian. incoming slash, at the end, is an argument: the thing the command acts on. The manual page summarises all of this in a synopsis line. Square brackets mean optional, and three dots mean the item may repeat. So ls, option repeated, file repeated, says that ls works with no options and no files at all, and with as many of each as you like. Now, where the help lives. man ls opens the manual page. But try man cd and Debian says there is no entry, because cd is not a program; it is part of Bash. For built-ins, ask Bash with help cd. Many GNU programs also print a quick summary with dash dash help. Finally, manual pages are split into numbered sections. Section one is user commands, five is file formats, seven is overviews, eight is administration commands. That matters when one name means two things. passwd in section one changes your password; passwd in section five describes the file that stores accounts. Last in this chapter: where your Linux is actually running.

Before going further, it is worth knowing exactly what kind of Linux you are sitting in, because the course's boot, kernel and service examples don't apply equally everywhere. The table compares four environments. A physical host runs its own kernel, and boots the way the previous sections described, from real firmware. A virtual machine does the same on virtual hardware: it has its own kernel and its own boot, and its own systemd as process one. A container is different in kind. It does not boot at all, and it has no kernel of its own. It is a group of ordinary processes on the host, given their own view of files, processes and network, and its first process is whatever command the image says to run, which is often the application itself, not systemd. WSL two, on Windows, runs a Linux kernel built by Microsoft inside a lightweight virtual machine that Windows starts for you. It runs systemd only when that is enabled. The code card makes the container case concrete. On a Debian thirteen host, uname dash r reports Debian's kernel. Inside an Alpine container on the same host, uname still reports Debian's kernel, because it is the same kernel, while os-release names Alpine, because those are the image's files. These are the two identities from the first section, now disagreeing. And one last boundary: macOS is not Linux. Many commands look the same, but the kernel and the tools underneath are different. Next chapter: files, paths, and the names commands act on.

Commands act on files, and every file is reached by a path: a list of directory names joined by slashes. The question is always where the path starts. An absolute path begins with a slash, the root of the tree, so slash etc slash hostname means the same file no matter where you are. A relative path has no leading slash, and it is resolved from the current directory, the one we met in chapter one. The table shows four paths written from the lab directory. incoming slash a dot csv simply continues downward. dot dot means the parent, so dot dot slash reportd slash app dot log climbs one level and comes straight back, which looks pointless but is legal and resolves to the same file. Single dot means the current directory itself. The session below the table moves around with cd. cd dot dot climbs, and cd dash returns to wherever you were before. Then there is tilde. Tilde is not part of the filesystem at all. Bash replaces it with your home directory before the command ever runs. That is why the two commands at the bottom behave differently. ls tilde slash lab works, because Bash expanded it. Put it in quotes, and Bash leaves it alone, so ls receives a literal tilde and looks for a directory with that name, which does not exist. Knowing which layer interprets a character will come back again and again in chapter three. Next: what the top-level directories are for.

Unlike systems that give each program its own folder, Linux sorts its single tree by the kind of data, and once you know the categories you can usually guess where something lives. slash etc holds configuration, mostly small text files that administrators edit. slash usr holds installed programs and libraries, and it is the package manager's territory, not yours. slash var holds data that grows or changes while the system runs: logs, caches, queues and the state of applications. slash home holds one directory for each person. Two more are worth knowing early because they are not disk files at all. slash run lives in memory and holds runtime state, such as process ID files and sockets, so it starts empty after every reboot. slash proc and slash sys are generated by the kernel on demand: reading a file there asks the kernel a question. The table in the middle applies the same rules to one program, the reportd service you will install in chapter six. Its code goes under slash opt, the place for add-on software. Its settings go under slash etc. The records it receives and the reports it writes are state, so they belong under slash var slash lib, and its log files under slash var slash log. And one Debian detail: since Debian twelve, the old top-level slash bin is just a symbolic link into slash usr, as the last card shows. Next: what a file actually carries besides its contents.

A file is more than its bytes. It also carries metadata: what type of object it is, how big, who owns it, who may read or write it, and when things happened to it. All of that lives in a structure called the inode, and, as the next sections show, the name is stored somewhere else entirely. The first card is ls dash l on the lab directory. Read the first character of each line. A dash is a regular file, d is a directory, and l is a symbolic link, which ls helpfully shows pointing at its target. Then come permissions, the link count, the owner and group, the size and the modification time. stat shows the same inode in full. It adds the inode number and the times, and there are three of them that people regularly confuse. Modify is when the content was last written. Change is when the metadata last changed, for example a chmod or a new hard link. And Birth is creation time, which only some filesystems record. So ctime, the change time, is not creation time, whatever its name suggests. Finally, file ignores the name and reads the first bytes of content to guess what kind of data it is. That matters, because nothing on Linux enforces extensions. A file called dot csv can contain anything, and a program with no extension at all is perfectly normal. When it matters, check the content. Next, the commands that create, copy, move and remove files.

Most file work comes down to four commands, and the useful skill is predicting exactly what each one changes. The session on the left runs inside the lab directory. mkdir dash p creates reports and scratch, making any missing parent directories and staying quiet if they already exist. cp copies app dot log into scratch. A copy is a brand new file: new inode, new bytes, and with dash p it keeps the original's times and permissions. mv then renames the copy. Within one filesystem, a move does not touch the data at all; it changes a name and keeps the same inode, which is why moving a huge file is instant. ls dash i proves it, printing inode numbers: the original and the copy have different ones, and the renamed file kept the copy's. Moving across filesystems is different, and becomes a copy followed by a delete. Now the dangerous part. cp and mv both overwrite an existing target without asking, and rm has no recycle bin. Once a name is removed, the shell offers no way back. So build some habits. Practise in disposable directories, like scratch here, named explicitly. Use dash i to be asked before each overwrite or removal, or dash b to keep a backup of whatever would be replaced. And before handing a wildcard pattern to rm, run ls with the same pattern and read what it matches. Next: what a name actually is, and why removing one may not free any space.

Here is the model that explains a lot of surprising behaviour. A directory is just a table of names, and each name points at an inode. The inode is the file: its metadata and its data. The name is only a way of reaching it. A hard link is a second name pointing at the same inode. The diagram shows the October twelfth report reachable from reports and from archive. Neither name is the original; they are equal, and the inode simply counts them, Links two. Hard links only work within one filesystem, and not for directories. A symbolic link is different in kind. It is a tiny file whose content is a path, and the kernel follows that path each time the link is used. It can point across filesystems and at directories, but it depends on the path still being there. The session shows the consequence. After removing reports slash oct twelve, the hard link in archive still reads the data, because the inode still has one name. The symbolic link called latest now points at a path that no longer exists, so it dangles: No such file or directory. And this brings us to object lifetime. The kernel frees an inode's data only when its link count reaches zero and no process still has the file open. That is why deleting a large log that a running program is writing to can free no space at all. The last lines of the session show exactly that: after removing big dot log, the file descriptor of the process still writing it points at the same file, now marked deleted. The name is gone; the file is not. Chapter eight returns to this when disks fill up. Next: how the kernel walks a path.

When a program opens slash var slash lib slash reportd slash state dot db, the kernel does not look up that string in one go. It walks it, one component at a time, as the numbered steps show. It starts at the root directory. It looks up var in the root. Here, var is a mount point: a whole separate filesystem, on a different disk, has been attached at that name. The walk carries on inside the new filesystem, and nothing in the path tells you that happened. Then it looks up lib, then reportd, and finally state dot db. At every directory along the way, the kernel checks that the caller has search permission, the x bit, on that directory. And if any component is a symbolic link, its stored path is spliced in and walked in turn. This model turns two confusing error messages into precise evidence. No such file or directory means some name along the path does not exist. Permission denied means a directory on the way could not be searched, even if the file itself would be readable. In the second example, sam's home directory is mode seven hundred, which Debian twelve and later use for new home directories, so the walk stops there. When access fails, check each parent directory in turn before changing anything on the file itself. Finally, findmnt dash dash target tells you which filesystem actually holds a path, which matters the moment one disk fills up and another does not. Next: viewing and editing text, and the invisible differences between files.

Configuration files, logs, scripts and the reportd records are all plain text, so you need tools to read and edit text safely. To read, use less. It pages through a file of any size without changing it; slash searches, and q quits. To edit, Debian installs two editors by default. nano is the friendly one, with its key commands listed along the bottom of the screen. vi is modal, harder at first, and present on almost every Unix-like system you will ever log in to, so it is worth learning the basics eventually. Now, the subtle part. Text is just bytes, plus an agreement about what they mean. One agreement is the encoding, and Debian assumes UTF-8. The other is how a line ends. Linux ends each line with a single newline character. Windows ends each line with a carriage return followed by a newline. Most of the time you cannot see the difference, and that is exactly the problem. The card in the middle shows a script written on a Windows machine. Running it fails with bad interpreter, and the error mentions slash bin slash bash followed by caret M. The kernel is looking for a program literally named bash plus a carriage return. file confirms it, reporting CRLF line terminators, and cat dash capital A makes the hidden character visible as caret M. One sed command strips it from the end of each line. When something looks right but fails, inspect the bytes. Next: finding files, and choosing the right tool to inspect them.

The last skill in this chapter is finding things, and then looking at them with the right tool. find walks a directory tree as it exists right now, and tests every entry against the conditions you give it. Read the first command left to right. Start at the lab directory. Match names ending in dot csv. Modified less than one day ago. Larger than one kibibyte. The tests are combined with AND, so only files passing all of them are printed. Notice the quotes around star dot csv. Without them, Bash would try to expand the pattern itself, against the current directory, before find ever saw it. That is chapter three's subject, but the habit starts here. The second command uses dash xtype l to list dangling symbolic links, like the one we created two sections ago. Because find walks the live tree, it is always accurate, but it can be slow on a large one. The alternative, plocate, searches a prebuilt index of file names. It is very fast, but only as current as its last update, and Debian does not install it by default. Once you have found a file, choose the inspection tool by the question you are asking, as the table shows. file for what kind of content, stat for size, owner and times, head and tail for the start and the end, less to read the whole thing safely, and od for the exact bytes. Start with the least invasive tool. That completes the filesystem. Next chapter: connecting commands together.

So far each command has printed straight to the terminal. In fact every process starts with three open file descriptors, numbered zero, one and two. Zero is standard input, where a program reads. One is standard output, for results. Two is standard error, for error messages and diagnostics. By default all three are connected to your terminal, which is why results and errors appear mixed together. Redirection lets the shell connect them somewhere else before the program even starts. Less than reads input from a file. Greater than sends standard output to a file, replacing it, and double greater than appends. Two greater than redirects standard error. Now the detail that catches everyone. Redirections are applied from left to right, and two greater than ampersand one does not mean join the streams forever. It means: make descriptor two point wherever descriptor one points right now. The table traces both orders. In the first, greater than out moves descriptor one to the file, then two is pointed at the same place, so both lines land in out. In the second, two is copied from one while one still points at the terminal, and only afterwards does one move to the file. The error stays on screen. The session below shows exactly that, using ls on one name that exists and one that doesn't, which conveniently produces one line on each stream. And slash dev slash null is a special file that discards anything written to it. Next: connecting one command's output to another's input.

The vertical bar joins commands into a pipeline. The shell starts every stage at the same time, as separate processes, and connects the standard output of each one to the standard input of the next. Data flows through as it is produced, without temporary files. Notice what is not connected: standard error. When grep can't open its file, its complaint goes straight to the terminal, not down the pipe. Every command also finishes with an exit status, a number from zero to two hundred and fifty-five. Zero means success. Anything else means some kind of failure, and what each value means is documented per command. Dollar question mark holds the status of the last command that ran. And this is where pipelines surprise people. The status of a pipeline is the status of its last stage. In the session, grep fails with status two because the file is missing, but wc happily counts zero lines and succeeds, so the whole pipeline reports success. A script checking dollar question mark would carry on as if nothing were wrong. Bash offers two remedies. The PIPESTATUS array records every stage's status, here two then zero. And set dash o pipefail makes the pipeline's status the rightmost non-zero one, so the failure surfaces. Both are Bash features, not portable shell. One more reading tip: non-zero is not always an error. grep returns one simply when nothing matched. Next: what Bash does to your command line before running anything.

When you press enter, Bash does not run your line as typed. It rewrites it first, in a fixed order, and most shell bugs come from forgetting one of these steps. The scene lists them. Brace expansion turns a, open brace, one comma two, close brace, into a one and a two. Tilde becomes your home directory. Then the dollar forms: variables, command substitution, which runs a command and inserts its output, and arithmetic. Then comes the dangerous step. Any result that was not inside double quotes is split into separate words wherever it contains spaces, tabs or newlines. After that, words containing star or question mark are matched against filenames. And finally, the quote characters themselves are removed, so the program never sees them. The session shows the consequences. The variable f holds a filename with a space. Unquoted, it splits into two words, store and zero seven dot csv, and ls looks for two files that don't exist. Quoted, it stays one argument and works. Single quotes go further: nothing inside them expands at all, which is why dollar HOME prints literally on the left and as a path on the right. The last example surprises people too. When a pattern matches no files, Bash, by default, passes it through unchanged, so ls receives a literal star dot txt. The rule of thumb that follows from all this: put double quotes around every variable expansion, unless you specifically want splitting. Next: variables, the environment, and how Bash finds commands.

Variables come in two flavours, and mixing them up is a classic source of it works in my terminal but not in the script. A plain assignment, like REPORT DIR equals a path, creates a shell variable. It exists only inside this one shell. The session proves it: a child bash, started with bash dash c, prints empty brackets because it never received the value. export marks the variable for the environment, and from then on every child process this shell starts gets a copy. That word copy matters. A child can change its own copy, but never its parent's, the same rule we met with cd. The environment also holds PATH, which is how Bash finds external commands. Bash first checks for an alias, then a shell function, then a built-in. Only if none matches does it search PATH, a colon-separated list of directories, from left to right, and run the first match it finds. type dash a lists every candidate, in order. The PATH shown is Debian's default for ordinary users. Notice what is missing from it: the current directory. That is why make-report, a script sitting in the lab directory, is reported as command not found, while dot slash make-report works, because it names the file directly. This is deliberate. If the current directory were searched, anyone able to drop a file called ls into a directory you visit could run code as you. Next: searching text with grep and regular expressions.

grep reads lines and prints the ones that match a pattern. It is the tool you will reach for most when reading logs. The first command finds ERROR in the lab's app dot log, and dash n adds the line number of each match. Other options you will use constantly: dash c to count matching lines instead of printing them, dash v to invert the match, and dash i to ignore case. Here is the trap. grep's pattern is a regular expression, and in regular expressions some characters are special. The dot matches any single character. So searching for v one dot two also matches v one dash two and v one seven two, and the count comes back as five, not two. When you mean literal text, say so with dash capital F, for fixed string. Then dot is just a dot, and the count is correct. Always put patterns in single quotes too, so Bash doesn't expand anything in them first. The table shows the regex pieces you will meet most: dot for any character, caret to anchor at the start of a line, square brackets for a set of characters, star for repetition, and alternation, which needs backslashes in basic syntax but not with dash capital E. Finally, locale. What a character class like upper case means, and how ranges sort, depends on your language settings. Setting L C underscore ALL equals C switches to plain byte matching, which is predictable and noticeably faster on large files. Next: sorting and counting.

This pipeline is the classic Unix move: small tools, each doing one job, joined together. The question is how many errors each store produced. grep keeps only the ERROR lines. cut dash d space dash f three keeps the third space-separated field, which is the store name. The first card shows the result: store zero seven, store twelve, store zero seven. Now count them with uniq dash c. You might expect two for store zero seven. Instead you get one, one, one. uniq only merges identical lines that are next to each other, and the two store zero seven lines are separated by store twelve. Sorting first puts identical lines together, and then uniq dash c counts each run correctly. A final sort dash r n orders the counts from highest to lowest. That ordering, sort then uniq, is worth memorising. tr belongs to the same family. It translates or deletes single characters, for example tr dash d backslash r strips the Windows carriage returns from chapter two. Every one of these tools assumes something about the data: one record per line, and fields separated by a single, unambiguous character. Real data often breaks that. The second card is a CSV file where the city field contains a comma inside quotes, which is perfectly legal CSV. cut has no idea about quotes, splits on that comma anyway, and returns a fragment. When the format has rules like quoting, stop using line tools and use a parser that understands it, such as Python's csv module. Next: sed and awk.

sed and awk are both small programming languages, and you only need a little of each to be productive. sed, the stream editor, reads lines, applies edits, and writes the result to standard output. Its workhorse is the substitute command: s, slash, pattern, slash, replacement. The first card fixes inconsistent store names, turning store seven and store zero seven into the same spelling. Because sed writes to standard output, the first run is just a preview, piped into head. Only when the output looks right does the second command use dash i to edit the file in place, and the dot bak suffix keeps a copy of the original. That backup is your rollback, as the listing shows. The pattern uses backslash question mark, a GNU extension, which is why the card says GNU sed. awk thinks in fields. Dash capital F comma splits each CSV line at commas, so dollar one is the store and dollar three is the record count. The program adds each count into an array keyed by store, and the END block, which runs after the last line, prints the totals: fifty for store zero seven, seventeen for store twelve. On Debian the default awk is mawk, and this program is plain POSIX awk, so it runs the same in GNU awk. Two boundaries. awk's for in loop has no defined order, so if order matters, pipe the result to sort. And once a sed or awk program grows past a few lines, it has become a real program, and deserves a real script. Next: filenames that break scripts.

Most tools assume filenames are tidy. Linux doesn't. A name can contain any byte except the slash and the NUL byte. Spaces, quotes, newlines and a leading dash are all legal, and sooner or later one of them will arrive in your incoming directory. Start with the leading dash. rm dash draft dot csv looks like a request to remove a file, but rm sees options: d, r, then a, which it doesn't know. GNU rm even suggests the fix. There are two. A double dash tells the command that options have ended and everything after is an argument. Or write dot slash in front, which makes it unmistakably a path. Next, lists of names. The table compares three ways of handing many files to another command. Looping over the output of ls breaks on spaces, on newlines, and on leading dashes, because that output is just text that the shell splits into words. A glob like dot slash star is safe, because Bash produces each matching name as one complete word; you then quote the variable when you use it. And when the list comes from find, use the NUL byte as the separator. Since NUL can never appear in a filename, it's the one delimiter that cannot be confused with data. find dash print zero writes names separated by NUL, and xargs dash zero reads them, or a Bash while loop with read dash d and an empty string. The flags are GNU find and Bash features. Last in this chapter: archives.

The last tool in this chapter packages files up. An archive bundles many files, along with their names, permissions and timestamps, into a single file. Compression makes that file smaller. tar does both, and three commands cover almost everything. The first creates an archive. Dash c for create, z for gzip compression, f for the archive's filename, and dash capital C to change into the lab directory first, so that names inside the archive start at reports, not at your home directory. The second command lists the archive without extracting anything: dash t for list, v for the details. Read this before every extraction, especially for archives you did not make yourself. The bottom of the scene says what you are looking for. Does everything sit under one top folder, or will hundreds of files spill into the current directory? Do any names start with a slash or contain dot dot, trying to escape the destination? And would anything overwrite files that already exist, which tar does silently? GNU tar strips leading slashes and dot dot components by default, which helps, but it is a safeguard, not a reason to skip the listing. Then extract with dash x, into a directory created for the purpose, named with dash capital C. A note on metadata. tar records owners and modes, but when an ordinary user extracts, the files belong to that user; only root restores the original owners. You'll see why in chapter four. That completes the toolkit. Next chapter: who runs a command, and how processes live.

Chapter one showed that you are a number to the kernel. This chapter builds on that, starting with where the number comes from. getent passwd learner prints the account record, as seven colon-separated fields. The name, an x meaning the password hash is kept separately in slash etc slash shadow, the user ID, the primary group ID, a comment field, the home directory, and the login shell. getent reads through every account source the system is configured to use, so it also finds accounts that aren't stored in slash etc slash passwd, such as ones from a directory server. Groups work the same way. getent group sudo shows group twenty-seven, and lists learner as a supplementary member. Every file, in turn, has exactly one owner and one group, which ls dash l shows in the third and fourth columns. The table shows how Debian divides the number space. Zero is root, the superuser. One to nine hundred and ninety-nine are system accounts, created for services rather than people, such as www-data for web servers, and later in this course, reportd. One thousand and up are people. Giving each service its own account is a design choice you will see again: if the service is compromised, the attacker gets only what that account can reach. And remember what the kernel actually compares. Not names, but numbers: your user ID, and every group ID you hold, primary and supplementary. Next, what those numbers are allowed to do.

Every file carries nine permission bits, in three sets of three. Read, write and execute, for the owner, for the group, and for everyone else. When you access a file, the kernel picks one set, the first that applies to you: the owner set if you own it, otherwise the group set if you are in its group, otherwise the last set. Only that set is used. On a file, the bits mean what you would expect. On a directory, they mean something different, and the table spells it out. Read lets you list the names inside. Write lets you create, rename and delete entries, which also needs execute. And execute means search: permission to pass through the directory and open things inside it by name. That has a consequence people find surprising. Deleting a file needs write permission on the directory that contains it, not on the file itself. Now the plan's illustration. learner cannot read a report under slash srv slash shared. The tempting fix is to chmod the file. Instead, namei dash l walks the path and prints every component's mode and owner. Slash and srv are fine. shared is mode seven fifty, owned by reportd, and learner is neither the owner nor in the group, so the last set applies, and it has no x. The walk stops there. The file's own mode was never the problem, and changing it would have done nothing. Finally, numeric modes: read is four, write two, execute one, added up per set, so seven fifty is r w x, r dash x, nothing. Next: the defaults, and the bits beyond these nine.

Three refinements complete the permission model. First, defaults. When a program creates a file, it usually asks for mode six six six, read and write for everyone, or seven seven seven for a directory. The process's umask then removes bits from that request. Debian's default umask is zero two two, which removes write for group and others, so new files come out six four four and new directories seven five five, as the table shows. A stricter umask, like zero seven seven, makes new files private by default. Second, access control lists. Owner, group and other is sometimes too coarse. Here the reportd service account needs to read the lab's incoming directory without being added to learner's group. setfacl dash m adds a named entry for exactly that user. setfacl dash d adds a default ACL, which new files created inside the directory will inherit. ls marks a file that has an ACL with a plus sign after its mode, so always look for it. And setfacl dash b removes every extra entry, which is the rollback. Third, the special bits. Set-user-ID on a program makes it run as the program file's owner; passwd uses it so that ordinary users can update the root-owned shadow file, in a controlled way. Set-group-ID on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group, which is useful for shared project areas. And the sticky bit, which you'll see on slash tmp, lets everyone create files there but only delete their own. Next: becoming root, briefly and accountably.

Administration needs root, the account with user ID zero, but logging in as root all day is a bad idea. sudo is the alternative: it runs one command as another user, usually root, and only after two separate checks. The first is authentication: proving you are learner, by typing learner's own password, not root's. The second is authorisation: the policy in slash etc slash sudoers decides whether learner may run this command, as this user. On Debian, members of the sudo group may run anything. And every use is recorded with who ran what, from where, which is the accountability that a shared root password never gives you. sudo dash l shows exactly what you are permitted. Now a trap that catches everybody once. sudo echo, then greater than slash etc slash motd, fails with permission denied, even though echo ran as root. Remember chapter three: the redirection is performed by your shell, as you, before sudo even starts. The fix is to pipe into sudo tee, so that the program opening the file is the one running as root. Note that the last line really does change a system file. Finally, root is less absolute than it sounds. Modern kernels split root's power into named capabilities, which a service can be given individually. Namespaces mean root inside a container is not root on the host. And mandatory access control, AppArmor on Debian, can refuse a root process that steps outside its profile. Chapter ten returns to all three. Next: what a process actually is.

Every command you have run so far became a process: a running program with its own memory, its own identity and its own set of open files. Here is how a new one is made, step by step. Bash, process twenty-two oh one, reads the line sort app dot log, greater than, sorted dot log. It calls fork, and the kernel makes a copy of Bash: process twenty-two forty, the child. For a moment, two nearly identical shells exist. In the child, Bash now performs the redirection, pointing descriptor one at sorted dot log. Then the child calls exec, which replaces the Bash program inside it with slash usr slash bin slash sort. Same process, same PID, different program. That ordering explains a lot of what you've already seen. The table lists what the child inherits, always as a copy. Your user and groups, so sort can read exactly what you can and nothing more. The exported environment, which is why export mattered in chapter three. The current directory, so relative names mean the same thing. And the open file descriptors, including the redirection the shell just set up, so sort simply writes to its standard output and never knows a file is involved. Because these are copies, nothing the child does to them reaches the parent, which is the cd story from chapter one once more. Every process also records its parent's ID, PPID. ps with dash dash forest uses it to draw the family tree. Next: controlling running processes with jobs and signals.

Processes need to be controlled from outside: paused, resumed and stopped. The mechanism is the signal, a small numbered notification that the kernel delivers to a process. The session shows Bash's job control. sleep three hundred with an ampersand runs in the background, and jobs lists it as job one. kill percent one sends it a signal, and jobs then reports it terminated. Next, make-report runs in the foreground, and pressing control Z stops it, pausing it rather than ending it. bg resumes it in the background, and fg would bring it back to the front. The table lists the signals you will actually send. Control C sends INT. kill, and systemctl stop, send TERM by default. HUP is sent when the terminal goes away. Control Z sends TSTP. All of these can be caught by the program, which is the point: on TERM, a well-written program finishes the current record, flushes its output, removes temporary files and exits cleanly. KILL is different. It cannot be caught or ignored at all. The process gets no chance to clean up, which is exactly why it should be your last resort, not your first. So the proportionate sequence is TERM, wait a little, and only then KILL. And even KILL is not instant. A process blocked inside the kernel, for example waiting on a stuck network filesystem, shows state D in ps, and it will not disappear until that kernel operation returns. Next: what happens after a process exits.

Exiting is only half of a process's ending. When a program finishes, it calls exit with a status number, and the kernel frees its memory and closes its files. But the status still has to be delivered to someone: the parent, which may want to know whether the child succeeded. So the kernel keeps a small entry for the child until the parent collects that status by calling wait. Collecting it is called reaping, and then the entry is gone. The row at the top shows the life cycle. In the session, Bash starts make-report in the background and saves its PID. wait on that PID blocks until the child finishes, and then dollar question mark holds its status, three, the code the script chose for invalid input. Between exiting and being reaped, a process is a zombie. ps shows it with state Z, and the command in angle brackets, defunct. A zombie holds no memory and uses no CPU; it is only a process table entry holding a number. That's why the next line achieves nothing: kill dash nine on a zombie does nothing, because the process has already exited. There is nothing left to kill. So a zombie is evidence about its parent. Look at its PPID, and find out why that program never calls wait. A few zombies are harmless; thousands can exhaust the process table. And if the parent itself exits, its orphaned children are adopted by process one, systemd, which reaps them promptly. Last in this chapter: the live evidence the kernel keeps about each process.

Everything this chapter has described, identity, descriptors, state and limits, can be observed directly, because the kernel publishes it under slash proc. Each running process has a directory there named after its PID, and its contents are generated at the moment you read them. Dollar dollar is Bash's own process ID, so ls dash l slash proc slash dollar dollar slash fd lists this shell's open file descriptors. Zero, one and two all point at the terminal device, exactly as chapter three described. For a service, that same listing shows every log file, network socket and pipe it holds open, which is how you'll find the deleted-but-open file from chapter two. The table lists other entries worth knowing: cmdline for exactly what was run, cwd for its current directory, environ for its environment, readable only by its owner or root, and limits. Limits are the second half of this section. The kernel enforces per-process resource limits, such as the maximum number of open files. Each has a soft limit, which applies right now, and a hard limit, the ceiling up to which an unprivileged process may raise its own soft limit. ulimit dash n shows this shell's: a soft limit of one thousand and twenty-four, and a much higher hard limit set by systemd. When a busy service reaches its soft limit, opening anything else fails with too many open files. And limits are inherited, so a service gets whatever its parent, or its unit file, gave it. That completes identity and processes. Next chapter: turning commands into reliable scripts.

This chapter turns the commands you've learned into make-report, a small script that summarises a day of incoming records. A script is just a text file of commands. Its first line, starting with hash bang, is called the shebang, and it tells the kernel which interpreter should run the file. Here it is slash bin slash bash. The lines after it name the two arguments the script expects, and the last line prints a diagnostic. Note the greater than ampersand two at the end: diagnostics go to standard error, so they never mix with the report on standard output. The table compares four ways to run the same file. Dot slash make-report asks the kernel to execute it, which needs the execute bit, set once with chmod plus x, and then the shebang decides the interpreter. bash make-report names the interpreter yourself, so no execute bit is needed. sh make-report looks equivalent, but on Debian sh is dash, a smaller, faster shell without Bash's extensions. A Bash script run that way either fails or, worse, behaves subtly differently. And source runs the file inside your current shell, not in a child, so any cd or variable it sets remains afterwards. That's sometimes what you want for configuration, but rarely for a tool. Inside the script, dollar one and dollar two are the arguments, dollar hash counts them, dollar zero is the script's own name, and quoted dollar at passes all of them on, each intact. Next: making decisions.

Scripts make decisions with if, and the key idea is that if does not evaluate an expression. It runs a command and looks at its exit status. Zero means true; anything else means false. A test is simply a command whose only job is to answer with a status. The block on the left is the start of make-report's real work: validating its inputs before touching anything. The first check uses double square brackets, Bash's test command, to compare dollar hash, the argument count, with two. If it's wrong, the script prints a usage line to standard error and exits with status two. The second check asks whether the input is a directory, with dash d, and whether it's readable, with dash r, and exits with status three if not. Using different statuses for different failures lets whatever runs this script, a person or a scheduler, tell them apart. The third check shows that any command can be a condition. grep dash q prints nothing, and its status says whether it found two commas in a row, meaning an empty field. The table lists the tests you will use most. Note that double equals compares strings, while dash e q and dash l t compare integers; mixing them up gives wrong answers without errors. And one shortcut deserves a warning. a and and b or or c looks like if-then-else, but c also runs when b fails. Use a real if when that matters. Next: loops and functions.

make-report needs to do the same thing for every CSV file in the input directory, which is what loops are for. for file in, followed by the input directory and star dot csv, gives the loop one complete filename per pass, spaces and all, because the glob produces whole words, as chapter three explained. There is one edge case. If the directory has no CSV files, Bash passes the pattern through literally, so the first line inside the loop checks that the file exists, and continue skips to the next pass if not. The work for each file lives in a function called summarise. A function is a command you define yourself. Inside it, dollar one is the function's own first argument, not the script's. The word local makes the variable file exist only inside the function. That matters more than it looks. Without local, every variable in a Bash script is global, so a function can silently overwrite a variable its caller was using. The loop calls summarise inside command substitution, captures the count, prints the filename and count, and adds the count to a running total, which is printed at the end. The double dollar parentheses do integer arithmetic. Finally, four ways to stop early, which are easily confused. continue moves on to the next item. break leaves the loop. return ends a function and sets its status. And exit ends the entire script, wherever it is called from. Next: getting arguments and input lines through a script intact.

Most shell script bugs have the same cause: a value that was one argument gets split into several on its way through the script. Bash has one correct form for each job, and this section collects them. The first card sets two arguments, store zero seven dot csv and store twelve dot csv, each with a space, and passes them to a tiny helper that prints each argument it receives between angle brackets. With quoted dollar at, it receives exactly two, intact. With unquoted dollar at, Bash re-splits them into four useless pieces. With quoted dollar star, it gets a single argument, everything joined together. So when a script hands its arguments to another command, the form is always quoted dollar at. The same principle applies to lists you build yourself. Don't store a list of filenames in one string and hope to split it later. Put it in an array: files equals, parentheses, the glob. Each element is one name. Quoted dollar, brace, files, square brackets at, brace, expands to all of them, unsplit, and the hash form counts them. Arrays are a Bash feature, not portable shell. Finally, reading input line by line. The correct form is while I F S equals nothing, read dash r. Setting IFS to empty stops read trimming leading and trailing spaces, and dash r stops it interpreting backslashes. Together they deliver each line exactly as written. And always state the format you expect, here one filename per line, because no line-based loop can handle a filename containing a newline. Next: what happens when something fails.

Without instructions, a Bash script carries on after a command fails, running the next line on whatever was left behind. The usual first step is set dash e u o pipefail. Dash e exits when a command fails and nothing checked it. Dash u treats a reference to an unset variable as an error, which catches typos. And pipefail, from chapter three, makes a failing pipeline stage count. These help, but dash e in particular has rules that surprise experienced people, and the table lists them. A failure does not stop the script if the command is an if or while condition, if it comes before and and or or or, or if it happens inside a function that was itself called from one of those places. So a perfectly reasonable if summarise then line disables dash e for everything summarise does. That's why the script on the left doesn't rely on dash e alone. Each important step ends with or or die, an explicit check that prints a message and exits. You can see exactly where failure is handled by reading the code. The other half is cleanup. The script creates a temporary working directory with mktemp dash d, and immediately sets a trap on EXIT that removes it. That trap runs however the script ends: success, a die, or an interrupt. The bottom card shows the interrupted run from the plan. Control C stops make-report half way, and the temporary directory is gone anyway. Every mktemp should be followed by its trap. Next: publishing results safely, and two runs at once.

Once make-report runs on a schedule, other programs will read its output, and they don't wait politely until it's finished. The table compares two ways of writing reports slash latest dot csv. Write it directly, and a reader that opens the file mid-run sees half a report; so does everyone after a crash. Instead, write to a temporary file in the same directory, and when it is complete, mv it over the target. On one filesystem, that rename replaces the name in a single step, so any reader sees either the complete old report or the complete new one, never a mixture. Note the details in the code. mktemp creates the temporary file next to the target, not in slash tmp, because a rename across filesystems becomes a copy and loses the atomic switch. mktemp also creates files readable only by their owner, mode six hundred, so the script sets the mode it actually wants before publishing. And there's a limit the plan insists on. Atomic is not durable. After a power cut, the rename may have reached the disk and the data not, or neither. Durability needs an explicit flush, which chapter eight explains. The other problem is two runs at once, say the timer and a person testing. Both would write and rename, and the results would interleave. The first two lines open a lock file on descriptor nine, and flock dash n takes an exclusive lock without waiting, so a second run exits with a clear message instead. Next: logging, safe reruns and retries.

Once a script runs unattended, three things will certainly happen to it. It will be interrupted, it will be rerun, and sooner or later it will run twice for the same day. Each of those should be harmless. Start with logging. The log function prints a timestamp and a message to standard error, and also hands the message to logger, which writes it to the system journal tagged make-report. When something goes wrong at three in the morning, the journal is where you'll look first, in chapter six. Next, idempotency: running the script twice should have the same effect as running it once. The loop gives each input file a done marker in a state directory, and skips files that already have one. The crucial detail is the order. The marker is written only after the file was processed successfully. Write it first, and a crash in between marks unfinished work as done. The same design gives you resumable partial completion. If the script dies after forty files out of a hundred, the next run processes only the remaining sixty. Finally, retries. Some failures are temporary: a busy disk, a network hiccup. The inner loop tries each file up to three times, waiting longer after each failure and logging every attempt, then gives up on that file and moves on. Two rules keep retries honest. Always bound them, and only retry what could succeed later. A malformed file will fail the same way every time. The bottom card is the morning after: the journal shows three attempts on store twelve and the give-up, and the state directory shows that a rerun will redo only that one file. Last in this chapter: handing the script to a scheduler.

The last step for make-report is handing it to the system to run on a schedule, which chapter six sets up with a systemd timer. Before that, it's worth knowing why scripts that work perfectly in your terminal so often fail the first time they run unattended. The table compares the two environments. Your terminal has your PATH, with any directories you've added. A scheduled job gets a minimal one: for cron, just slash usr slash bin and slash bin. Your shell is wherever you last used cd; a scheduled job starts in slash or in the home directory. There's no terminal, so anything that asks a question either waits forever or fails. And output goes to a log, or to mail, or nowhere, unless something captures it. So prepare the script. Use absolute paths for every file it reads and writes. Never prompt; fail with a message to standard error and a distinct status instead. And make the exit status meaningful, because the scheduler and its logs are how you'll learn about failures. The second table answers a question every script eventually raises: should this still be shell? Shell is excellent at running other programs, joining them in pipelines, and moving files around. It is poor at parsing structured formats like CSV and JSON properly, at data structures and arithmetic, and at being tested. When the job is mostly the second kind, or the script passes a hundred lines or so, rewrite it in Python. That completes scripting. Next chapter: software, boot, and services.

Chapter six turns reportd into software that the system installs, starts and supervises. It begins with packages. A package bundles a program's files with metadata: its version, what it depends on, and small scripts that run when it is installed or removed. Packages come from repositories, and Debian 13 describes them in files under slash etc slash apt slash sources dot list dot d, using the deb822 format shown at the top. Each source names a URL, the suites to use, such as trixie and trixie-updates, the components, and, crucially, the signing key that its contents must be signed with. The middle of the scene shows how a download is checked. apt update fetches the InRelease file, which is signed by the archive key installed on your system. That file lists cryptographic hashes of the package indexes. Each index, in turn, lists the hash of every package file. So when apt downloads a dot deb, it can verify that file against a chain that ends in a signature it trusts. A mirror, a proxy or an attacker on the network can serve you old or missing files, but cannot forge new ones. That tells you exactly what you are trusting: the signer. And because package scripts run as root during installation, adding any third-party repository gives its signer the power to run code as root on your machine. Treat it as that kind of decision. Next: reading a package transaction before making it.

apt is the tool you use to change installed software, and the habit to build is reading its plan before agreeing to it. apt install dash dash simulate jq asks for the plan without changing anything, and doesn't even need root. Debian thirteen ships apt version three, with this tidier layout. It will install jq, two libraries it depends on, and nothing will be removed. That last line is the one to check every time. A transaction that quietly removes something important is the classic way to break a server. Only then run the real command with sudo. The table lists the verbs. apt update refreshes the package indexes from the repositories; it installs nothing. apt upgrade installs newer versions of what you already have. apt remove uninstalls a program but keeps its configuration files, in case you reinstall it. apt purge deletes the configuration as well. That distinction exists because Debian protects configuration. Files that a package installs under slash etc are marked as conffiles. When an upgrade brings a new version of a conffile you have edited, your version is kept, and apt asks you what to do rather than overwriting it. Underneath apt is dpkg, the lower-level tool that actually installs package files, and it can answer two questions apt can't easily answer. dpkg dash capital L lists every file a package installed, and dpkg dash capital S tells you which package owns a given file. Next: what happens between power-on and systemd, in more detail.

In chapter one, the boot was a list of handoffs. Now that you're responsible for a system, you need to know where each stage lives, because the error you see tells you which one broke. The table pairs them up. UEFI firmware lives on the machine itself; if it finds nothing bootable, it says so before Linux is involved at all. GRUB lives on the EFI system partition and in slash boot slash grub; if its own files are damaged, you land at a grub rescue prompt. The kernel and the initramfs are files in slash boot. A kernel that can't start halts with a panic. An initramfs that can't find the root filesystem drops you into a minimal initramfs shell. And if the root filesystem is found but something listed for mounting fails, systemd starts emergency mode. On a running system, two pieces of evidence matter. slash proc slash cmdline shows exactly what GRUB passed to the kernel, including root equals UUID, which is how the initramfs knows which disk to mount. And slash boot shows the installed kernels. Debian keeps the previous one when a new kernel is installed, each with its own initramfs. That gives you the first recovery path: if a new kernel misbehaves, pick the older one from GRUB's advanced menu. The second is editing the kernel line at the menu and adding systemd dot unit equals rescue dot target, which boots to a root shell with almost nothing started. Both need console access, so make sure you have it before you need it. Next: what systemd manages once it's running.

Once the kernel starts systemd as process one, systemd manages everything else as units. A unit is a named object of a particular type, described by a small text file, with declared relationships to other units. The scene lists the types you will meet. A service is a process that systemd starts and supervises: reportd will be one. A timer starts a service on a schedule, a socket starts a service when someone connects, and a path unit starts a service when a file appears or changes. A mount unit represents a mounted filesystem. And a target is a named group of units, used as a goal state. systemctl get-default shows the target the system boots towards: multi-user dot target, a complete system without a graphical desktop, which is normal for servers. graphical dot target includes everything in multi-user plus a desktop, and rescue dot target, from the previous section, includes almost nothing. When reportd's unit says it is wanted by multi-user dot target, it is joining that group. systemctl list-units lists what's loaded and its state. Here, cron and the SSH server are active and running. Notice also that there are two kinds of manager. The system manager is process one, runs as root, and manages services for the whole machine. Each logged-in user also gets their own user manager, reached with systemctl dash dash user, which can run personal services and timers without any root access. Next: writing reportd's own unit file.

Here is reportd's unit file. It has three sections. Unit holds a description and relationships to other units. Service says how to run it: as the reportd account, with this command line and configuration file. And Install says what enable should do, here: add reportd to multi-user dot target. Where the file lives matters. Units installed by packages live under slash usr slash lib slash systemd, and you should never edit those, because the next upgrade replaces them. Local units and local changes go under slash etc slash systemd slash system, which takes precedence. To change one setting, don't copy the whole file. sudo systemctl edit reportd creates a drop-in, a small file holding only your change, here an environment variable for the listen address. systemctl cat then shows the unit file and every drop-in, in the order they apply, which is the first thing to check when a service doesn't behave as its file suggests. Now the most misunderstood pair of directives, and the table spells them out. After equals B only controls order. If both units are being started anyway, this one waits for B. It does not cause B to be started. Wants equals B does cause B to start, but doesn't wait for it. Requires is stronger: if B stops, this unit stops too. So the usual combination is Wants plus After, exactly as reportd uses for network dash online dot target, the target that means networking is actually configured, not merely that the network service has started. Next: starting, enabling, and when a service is really ready.

systemctl has several verbs that sound alike, and mixing them up causes most surprises with services. The table lists them. start runs the service now, and that's all; after a reboot it won't be running. enable creates a symlink so the service starts at boot, and, importantly, does not start it now. The session shows it. After enable, is-active still says inactive. enable dash dash now does both at once. The two reloads are different again. daemon-reload tells systemd itself to re-read unit files, which you need after editing one by hand; systemctl edit does it for you. reload asks the application to re-read its own configuration, usually by sending it a signal, without stopping it. restart stops and starts it, with a short interruption. Then readiness, which the plan singles out. In the session, start succeeds and curl immediately fails to connect. Nothing is broken. With the default service type, simple, systemd considers the service started the moment the process exists. But reportd still has to load its configuration and open its listening socket, and a request arriving in that window fails. Units that depend on reportd with After are released at the same moment, and hit the same problem. The fix is in the program and the unit together. With Type equals notify, the program tells systemd when it's actually ready, and only then is the unit marked active. So when a service reports active, ask which kind of active it means. Next: reading a service's logs.

Services have no terminal, so their output goes to the journal, the log managed by systemd. Every line is stored with the unit that produced it, the boot it happened in, and a priority, so you can ask precise questions. Here's the plan's failed start. systemctl status shows the service failed, and the Process line has the key detail: status two hundred and seventeen, slash USER. journalctl dash u reportd, dash b for this boot, dash p warning for warnings and worse, shows systemd's own explanation: it failed to determine user credentials. The unit says User equals reportd, and that account doesn't exist yet. The fix is the adduser command on the last line, creating reportd as a system account with its home in slash var slash lib slash reportd. Notice how the evidence chain runs from status, to the journal, to an identity problem from chapter four. Applications may also write their own log files, and reportd writes under slash var slash log slash reportd. Those need rotation, or they grow until the disk is full, and logrotate does it from small configuration files. This one rotates weekly, keeps eight old files, and compresses them. The postrotate step matters most. After logrotate renames the current file, reportd still holds it open and keeps writing to it. Sending it HUP tells it to reopen its log by name. Skip that, and when the old file is eventually deleted, you have chapter two's deleted-but-open file, quietly using disk space. The journal itself is size-capped and rotates automatically. Next: running things on a schedule.

Chapter five prepared make-report to run unattended. Here is the scheduler. With systemd, a schedule is two units. The timer says when: OnCalendar, every day at two in the morning. The service it starts says what: a oneshot service, meaning it runs a command to completion rather than staying up, as the reportd account, with absolute paths for both arguments. systemctl list-timers shows when it last ran and when it will run next. A few settings change the semantics in ways worth choosing deliberately. Persistent equals true means that if the machine was off at two o'clock, the run happens shortly after the next boot instead of being skipped. RandomizedDelaySec adds a random delay of up to five minutes, which matters when hundreds of machines share one schedule and one database. And a timer never starts a second copy of its service while the first is still running, which removes one of the races from chapter five. The bottom of the scene compares this with cron, the traditional scheduler, still widely used. The cron line is shorter: minute, hour, day, month, weekday, user, command. But a run missed while the machine is off is simply skipped, output goes to mail if anything is configured to deliver it, the environment is cron's minimal PATH, and nothing stops two runs overlapping. Either can be the right choice; what matters is knowing which guarantees you're relying on. Last in this chapter: giving reportd only the privileges it needs.

A unit file can do much more than start a program. It can limit what the program can touch, how much it can use, and what it can become. This is least privilege from chapter four, applied by the service manager. Start with identity. reportd runs as its own account, never as root. StateDirectory and LogsDirectory tell systemd to create slash var slash lib slash reportd and slash var slash log slash reportd, owned by that account, so the package doesn't need to set permissions by hand. Next, supervision. Restart equals on-failure restarts reportd if it crashes, after a five second delay. systemd also has a start limit: if a unit fails repeatedly in a short window, it stops trying, so a broken configuration doesn't loop forever. Then resources, enforced by the kernel's control groups, which chapter nine examines. MemoryMax caps reportd's memory. If it exceeds that, the kernel's out-of-memory killer acts inside reportd's group only, instead of picking a victim from the whole machine. CPUQuota is a ceiling, not a guarantee. Finally, the sandbox. ProtectSystem equals strict makes the entire operating system read-only to reportd, except the directories it was given. ProtectHome hides home directories completely. PrivateTmp gives it its own temporary directory, and NoNewPrivileges stops it gaining privileges through set-user-ID programs. systemd-analyze security scores what remains exposed. Treat that number as a prompt for review, not a verdict. That completes software and services. Next chapter: reaching reportd over the network.

Chapter seven follows a request from a client to reportd and back, and it starts with addresses. A host talks to the network through interfaces, and ip address lists them. The first, lo, is loopback: a virtual interface for traffic that never leaves this machine, with the addresses one twenty-seven dot zero dot zero dot one and colon colon one. The second, enp one s zero, is a real network card. Its flags say it's up and has a link, and its link slash ether line shows its hardware address. Below that are the addresses that matter. inet is IPv4, here one nine two dot one six eight dot one dot twenty, slash twenty-four. inet6 is IPv6, and this interface has two of them, which is completely normal. The slash twenty-four is the prefix length, and the table reads it. The first twenty-four bits name the network, one nine two dot one six eight dot one; the last eight name this host on it. Every address sharing that prefix is on-link: this host can reach it directly, with no router in between. The other addresses fall into three kinds. Loopback addresses are reachable only from this host itself, which is why reportd will listen on one. Global addresses can be routed across networks. And link-local IPv6 addresses, starting f e eight zero, exist on every IPv6 interface, but only work on the directly attached link. Next: how a packet for somewhere else finds its way out.

Once a packet has a destination address, the kernel has to decide where to send it next, and that is the routing table's job. ip route shows a typical table. The second line covers the local subnet: anything in one nine two dot one six eight dot one dot zero slash twenty-four is reached directly through enp one s zero. The first line is the default route: anything else goes via one nine two dot one six eight dot one, the gateway, a router that knows how to reach other networks. The kernel's rule is longest prefix match. Among all the routes whose prefix contains the destination, the most specific wins. The default route, zero dot zero dot zero dot zero slash zero, contains every address, so it matches everything but wins only when nothing more specific does. You don't need to work this out by hand. ip route get asks the kernel what it would do for one address. A neighbour on the subnet is delivered directly, out of enp one s zero. A public address like nine dot nine dot nine dot nine goes via the gateway. One caution belongs here, because it explains many connection problems. Having a route is not the same as being reachable. The reply has to find its way back, so the far end needs a route to you. And every router along the path makes its own decision, with its own table. A missing route anywhere, in either direction, looks like a timeout from where you sit. Next: what is actually listening when a packet arrives.

An IP address gets a packet to the right host. A port number gets it to the right program on that host. A program that wants to receive connections opens a socket, binds it to an address and port, and listens. There are two transports you'll meet constantly. TCP sets up a connection, and delivers data in order, acknowledging it and retransmitting anything lost. Web traffic and SSH use TCP. UDP sends independent datagrams with none of that machinery: no connection, no ordering, no retries. DNS queries typically use UDP. ss shows sockets. With dash l n t p, it lists listening TCP sockets, numerically, with the owning process, which needs root to see other users' processes. Two programs are listening here. reportd listens on one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one, port eighty eighty. sshd listens on zero dot zero dot zero dot zero, port twenty-two, and again on the IPv6 equivalent. The address in front of the port is the bind address, and as the table shows, it decides who can connect at all, before any firewall is consulted. Bound to loopback, reportd accepts connections only from programs on this same host. Bound to one interface address, it accepts anything that can route to that address. Bound to zero dot zero dot zero dot zero, or square brackets colon colon, it listens on every address the host has. reportd's loopback binding is deliberate, and section nine shows why. Next: turning names into addresses.

People type names, but packets need addresses, so almost every connection begins with name resolution. A program doesn't usually speak DNS itself. It asks the C library, and the library follows slash etc slash nsswitch dot conf. On a Debian server, the hosts line says files, then dns. Files means slash etc slash hosts, a local table that is checked first. Only if the name isn't there does the library ask a DNS server, the one named in slash etc slash resolv dot conf. That server either knows the answer or asks others, and caches what it learns for as long as the record's time-to-live allows. The session shows why the order matters. getent hosts follows exactly the same path that curl, ssh and reportd will use, and it returns ten dot zero dot zero dot ninety-nine. dig asks the DNS server directly, skipping slash etc slash hosts, and returns one nine two dot one six eight dot one dot twenty. Two tools, two different answers. The grep reveals the cause: a forgotten test entry in slash etc slash hosts, overriding DNS for every program on this machine. dig is in the bind nine dnsutils package and is excellent for investigating DNS itself, but to know what your programs will actually connect to, trust getent. And remember caches. After a DNS record changes, clients and servers may keep the old answer until its time-to-live expires, so a fix can be correct and still not visible yet. Next: where network configuration lives, and what survives a reboot.

There are two layers to network configuration, and confusing them leads to changes that vanish. The kernel holds the current state: the addresses, routes and settings in effect right now. ip can change that state directly. The first card adds a second address to enp one s zero, and it works immediately. The next line removes it again, which is the rollback to keep next to every runtime change. But even if you don't remove it, the address is gone after the next reboot, or the next time the interface is restarted, because nothing recorded it. Runtime changes are for testing. Persistence belongs to a network manager, a program that reads configuration files at boot and recreates the state. The second card is the classic Debian server configuration, from the ifupdown package, in slash etc slash network slash interfaces. It brings enp one s zero up automatically and asks DHCP for its settings. DHCP, the dynamic host configuration protocol, lets a server on the network hand out the address, the default gateway and the DNS server to use, so they don't have to be written on each machine. IPv6 here uses router advertisements instead. The table lists the three managers you'll meet on Debian. ifupdown on servers, NetworkManager on desktops and laptops, and systemd-networkd on many cloud images. Each has its own files, and an interface should belong to exactly one. So before editing anything, find out which manager is in charge of the interface, and change its configuration rather than another's. Next: diagnosing a failed request, layer by layer.

When someone says they can't reach reportd, the most useful thing you can do is read the exact error, because each kind of failure points at a different layer. The card shows four attempts with curl. The first fails with could not resolve host. No packet was ever sent to reportd; name resolution failed, and here the reason is a typo in the name. The second fails almost instantly with couldn't connect. A fast failure like that usually means the host was reached and actively refused the connection, because nothing was listening on that address and port. And look closely: the client used the host's network address, but reportd listens only on loopback, as section three showed. Nothing is broken; it's configured that way. The third waits five seconds and gives up. A timeout means packets disappeared somewhere: no route, a firewall silently dropping them, or a host that's down. It tells you something on the path is wrong, but not which hop. The fourth succeeds at the network level completely. The server answered with HTTP five oh three, an application error. The network is fine; look at reportd's logs. The table summarises what each suggests, and, just as important, what it does not prove. Treat each as a hypothesis about a layer, then test that layer. And be careful with ping. Many networks filter its packets, so a failed ping proves very little about whether a service is reachable. Test the real port with the real protocol. Next: logging in to remote machines safely.

SSH is how you will administer reportd's host remotely, and its security rests on checking two identities, in a fixed order. First, the server proves who it is. Every SSH server has a host key, and the first time you connect, your client has nothing to compare it with, so it shows you the key's fingerprint and asks. This is the moment that matters. Compare the fingerprint with one you got another way, for example from the administrator, or from the console of a machine you just built. If it matches, accept, and the key is saved in known hosts, then checked silently on every later connection. Only then do you prove who you are. Passwords work, but keys are better. ssh-keygen creates a key pair. The private half stays on your machine, ideally protected by a passphrase, and ssh-copy-id installs the public half on the server. An agent can hold your unlocked key for the session, so you type the passphrase once. Three habits are worth refusing to form. If SSH warns that a host key has changed, stop and find out why.
