It may be a reinstalled server, or it may be someone in the middle. Never switch host key checking off to make a warning go away, because that removes the first check entirely. And don't forward your agent to machines you don't fully trust: anyone with root there can use your keys while you're connected. Next: running commands and copying files over SSH.

Logging in interactively is only one way to use SSH. ssh followed by a host and a command runs that one command remotely and returns its output, which is how scripts and other tools work with remote machines. The trap is that your command line is parsed twice: first by your local shell, then by the shell on the remote machine. Chapter three's expansion rules apply at both ends, and quoting decides which end does what. In the first row of the table, tilde and star are unquoted, so your local shell expands them first: tilde becomes your home directory on your own machine, and the star is matched against your own files. What reaches the remote machine is the result. In the second row, the single quotes protect everything from your local shell, so the remote shell expands tilde and star against the remote machine's files. That is almost always what you mean. For copying files, rsync is the tool to learn. It copies only what has changed, preserves modes and times with dash a, and can run as a dry run first, listing exactly what it would transfer. Note the trailing slash on the source: it means the directory's contents, not the directory itself, which is the most common rsync surprise. Finally, if you run many short commands against the same host, each one pays for a full login. ControlMaster in your SSH configuration keeps the first connection open and reuses it for the rest. Last in this chapter: who can reach reportd at all.

The last question is who can reach reportd at all, and the answer is a series of independent controls, any of which can stop a request. The diagram follows a public request in order. An upstream firewall, a home router or a cloud provider's security group, allows only port four four three through. The host's own firewall, written in nftables, Debian's firewall framework, allows SSH and HTTPS in and drops everything else. The ruleset below it is a minimal illustration: drop by default, accept replies to connections this host started, accept loopback, accept ports twenty-two and four four three. Then a reverse proxy listens on four four three. It terminates TLS, meaning it holds the certificate and decrypts the request, and forwards it to reportd over loopback. And reportd itself is still bound to one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one. That's the design reason from section three. reportd is unreachable from outside by construction, not just because a firewall rule happens to block it. If a rule is ever deleted by mistake, reportd is still not exposed. Only the proxy faces the network, and TLS protects the request in transit as far as the proxy. When debugging, remember that every layer can block traffic, and a timeout from section six could come from any of them. Finally, the plan's warning. A firewall or SSH change can lock you out of the machine you're changing. Keep your existing session open, test from a second one, and know your console path before you start. Next chapter: where reportd's data actually lives.

Chapter eight is about where reportd's data actually lives, starting with the disks themselves. When the kernel discovers a storage device, a driver gives it a name, like s d a for a SATA disk or n v m e zero n one for an NVMe drive, and a device file appears under slash dev. The catch is that these names are handed out in discovery order. Add a disk, move a cable, or let two controllers race at boot, and yesterday's s d b can become today's s d c. Anything that refers to a disk by that name can suddenly point at the wrong one. That's why udev exists. When a device appears, udev reads its identifiers, such as the model and serial number, and the UUID of any filesystem on it, and creates symbolic links under slash dev slash disk that don't change. The card shows two of them. The by-id links are named after the physical disk's model and serial, so they follow the hardware wherever it's plugged in. blkid shows the filesystem's UUID, a random identifier written when the filesystem was created, so it follows the filesystem, even if it's copied to another disk. The table turns that into a rule. Kernel names are fine for a quick look right now. To choose a physical disk, for example one to replace, use by-id. And for anything that must survive a reboot, especially slash etc slash fstab, use UUID. Next: the layers between a path and a disk.

On a simple machine, a disk holds partitions and each partition holds a filesystem. Real servers often stack more layers in between, and lsblk shows them as a tree. Read this one from the top. One NVMe disk has three partitions. The first is the small EFI system partition from chapter six, mounted at slash boot slash efi. The second holds slash boot. The third is encrypted with LUKS, and when it's unlocked at boot it appears as a new block device, the crypt row. That device is in turn a physical volume for LVM, which carves it into logical volumes: one for the root filesystem, and one for slash var. Every layer is a block device built on the one beneath it. Now trace a path down through the stack, as the plan asks. findmnt dash capital T, given reportd's state directory, reports the mount that contains it: slash var, on the logical volume vg zero dash var. So reportd's data passes through a filesystem, a logical volume, an encryption layer, a partition and finally the disk, as the diagram below lays out. That matters for two reasons. Each layer has its own way of failing and its own tools: an encrypted volume that won't unlock is a different problem from a filesystem error. And capacity belongs to a single filesystem. When slash var fills up, slash may have plenty of room, and reportd still can't write. Next: filesystems, mount options, and fstab.

A filesystem is the structure that turns a block device into named files and directories: ext4 here, which is Debian's default. To use one, it has to be mounted, attached to the directory tree at a mount point, and slash etc slash fstab lists the mounts to make at every boot. The first card adds a data disk for archived reports. Each line has six fields: the device, by UUID as the previous section recommended, the mount point, the filesystem type, a comma-separated list of options, and two numbers for the old dump tool and for the order of filesystem checks at boot. On a systemd system, each line is turned into a mount unit, so the same dependency machinery from chapter six applies. The options deserve thought. nofail means that if this disk is missing at boot, the system carries on without it. Without it, a missing data disk stops the whole boot. noexec, nodev and nosuid refuse to run programs, honour device files, or apply set-ID bits from this filesystem, which is sensible for a disk that only stores data. ro mounts it read-only. Then apply it carefully, because fstab mistakes surface at the worst moment: the next reboot. findmnt dash dash verify checks the file for syntax errors, unknown UUIDs and wrong types. daemon-reload regenerates the mount units, and mounting it now lets you confirm the options took effect, as the last line shows. A broken line without nofail drops the next boot into emergency mode, needing the console. Next: when the disk fills, and the numbers don't agree.

reportd starts failing with no space left on device, and the investigation shows why you should know exactly what each tool measures. df dash h reports slash var completely full: one hundred and eighty-six gigabytes used. df dash i counts inodes, the per-file records from chapter two, and only four percent are used, so it isn't a flood of tiny files. Then du dash s h adds up everything it can reach under slash var by name, and finds only seventy-one gigabytes. Over a hundred gigabytes are unaccounted for. The table lists the usual reasons df and du disagree. The first is the one from chapters two and six: a file that has been deleted but is still held open. Its blocks are still allocated, so df counts them, but it has no name, so du can't see it. lsof plus L one lists open files with no remaining links, and here it is: reportd still writing to a log file that someone deleted, now a hundred and fifteen gigabytes. Restarting reportd, or telling it to reopen its logs, releases the space. The second reason is files hidden under a mount point. If data was written into a directory before another filesystem was mounted on top of it, those files still use space, but no path reaches them until you unmount. The third is ext4's reserved blocks, kept back for root by default. And the reverse case exists too. If inodes run out, writes fail even with gigabytes of free blocks. Quotas can also cap a single user or group. Next: pooling disks, and what redundancy does not protect.

Two technologies often sit in the storage stack, and they solve different problems. LVM, the logical volume manager, is about flexibility. Disks or partitions become physical volumes, they're pooled into a volume group, and logical volumes are carved out of the pool. The payoff is in the card. When slash var runs short, vgs shows the free space left in the group, and lvextend dash dash resizefs grows the logical volume and the filesystem on it in one step, while it's mounted. RAID is about surviving hardware failure. In RAID one, every write goes to two disks, so when one dies, the other carries on with no downtime and no data lost. Here is the contrast the plan insists on, and the table lays it out. Ask what survives each failure. A dead disk? The mirror survives it, and so does a backup. Now an administrator runs rm dash r f on the wrong directory. The mirror faithfully deletes the files on both disks, immediately. Same for an application that writes bad data, or corruption from a bug. And both disks share a failure domain: the same server, the same room, the same attacker. A fire, a theft or ransomware on the host takes both. A backup survives all of these, but only because it is independent of the original, older than the mistake, and stored somewhere else. So redundancy keeps the service running through a hardware fault. A backup is what lets you recover from everything else. Next: what a successful write actually promises.

Chapter five promised to explain why an atomic rename isn't the same as durability. Here's why. When a program writes to a file and write returns successfully, the data is usually not on the disk yet. The kernel has copied it into the page cache, a large area of memory holding file data, and marked those pages dirty. A few seconds later, the kernel writes them back to the device in the background, and even then the disk may hold them in its own volatile cache for a while. The diagram shows the four places one write passes through. That design makes most programs fast, but it means three different claims must be kept apart, as the table does. Write succeeded only says the kernel accepted the bytes. If the power fails now, they may be gone. The data was flushed is a stronger claim, and the program gets it by calling fsync on the file, which doesn't return until the data has reached stable storage. And for the write-then-rename pattern, the rename itself is a change to the directory, so the directory needs an fsync too before the new name is durable. Databases do all of this carefully; simple scripts usually don't. The page cache also explains a common misreading of free. Here buff slash cache is eleven gigabytes and free is just one point two, which looks alarming. It isn't. Cache is given back the moment programs need memory, which is why available, at twelve gigabytes, is the column to read. Swap holds pages moved out of RAM under real pressure, which is chapter nine's subject. Next: snapshots, backups, and consistency.

A backup is only worth what you can restore from it, and that depends on how it was taken. The table contrasts two methods. An LVM or filesystem snapshot captures every block at one instant, which is quick and convenient. But if a database was in the middle of a transaction at that instant, the snapshot contains exactly what a sudden power cut would have left. That's called crash-consistent. The database will probably recover from it, but it has to go through its crash recovery to do so, and not every application can. The alternative is to ask the application itself for a backup. Then you get a state the application vouches for, ready to use as it is: application-consistent. The card is reportd's nightly backup. sqlite3's dot backup command takes a consistent copy of the state database while reportd keeps running. tar archives the reports directory, as in chapter three. And rsync copies both to another host, because a backup on the same machine shares that machine's fate, as the previous section showed. Retention is the other half. Keeping only last night's copy is not enough, because mistakes are often noticed late. Keep several generations: here seven daily and four weekly, so you can go back to before last month's bad change. Keep at least one copy away from the host, and ideally away from the site. And remember chapter ten's point now: a backup you haven't restored from is a hope, not a plan. Last in this chapter: when storage fails.

Finally, what to do when storage actually fails. The evidence usually arrives in the kernel log first. The card shows two kinds. The first line is from the NVMe driver: an I/O error reading a block, which means the device itself failed a request. The second is from ext4, which hit a problem reading a directory. smartctl, from the smartmontools package, asks the drive for its own health assessment, and this one reports failed. Together that points at failing hardware, not just a damaged filesystem. Repair is something to rehearse before you need it, and the plan is explicit that you shouldn't practise on real disks. The middle card creates a disposable filesystem inside a one hundred megabyte file in the lab directory. e2fsck can check it like a real disk. The dash n flag opens it read-only and answers no to every proposed fix, so you can see what it would change before letting it change anything. Then dash y applies the repairs. On a real system, the order in the bottom box matters. Stop writing, and unmount the filesystem: repairing a mounted filesystem can destroy it. If the disk itself is failing, every read stresses it further, so copy the whole device to healthy storage first and repair the copy. Check before fixing. And keep in mind that repair and restore are different things. fsck makes a filesystem consistent again, which can mean discarding damaged files. Often the faster, safer path is a fresh filesystem and a tested restore. Next chapter: diagnosing resource problems systematically.

Chapter nine is about finding out why a system misbehaves, and it follows one incident from start to finish. Since Tuesday, the reports page has been slow. The method begins with four questions, and it's worth writing the answers down. The symptom, as users experience it and measured: the ninety-fifth percentile response time is eight seconds, it used to be zero point four, and some requests now fail with five oh three. The timeline: it started on Tuesday around two in the morning, and it's worst at nine, when people arrive. The baseline: last week, under the same load, the same page took zero point four seconds. Without a baseline, you can't tell whether a number is unusual. Then, hypotheses, deliberately more than one. The table lists four candidate explanations. The CPU could be saturated. The machine could be short of memory. The disk could be slow. Or Tuesday's change could be the cause. The useful thing about writing them down this way is the middle column: each hypothesis predicts specific evidence, and the last column says how to look for it. A good next step is the check that separates hypotheses, rather than one that would fit all of them. And resist the urge to settle on the first explanation that seems plausible. Keep the others alive until evidence actually contradicts them. The next five sections take one resource at a time, on this same incident, starting with the CPU.

The first suspect is usually the processor, and two numbers get confused here more than anywhere else. CPU utilisation says what the processors spent their time doing. top's CPU line breaks it down. us and sy are time running user programs and the kernel. id is idle. wa is also idle, but idle while at least one task was waiting for input or output. And st, on a virtual machine, is time the hypervisor gave to someone else. Load average is a different measure. It's an average number of tasks that wanted to run, over one, five and fifteen minutes. On Linux, it counts not only tasks that are running or waiting for a CPU, but also tasks in uninterruptible sleep, state D from chapter four, which usually means waiting on a disk. That's why the card compares two hosts with eight cores and the same load of about eight. Host A is CPU-bound: ninety-one percent user time, almost nothing idle. Its load really is eight busy processors. Host B has a load of eight with forty-one percent idle and fifty-four percent waiting on I/O. Its processors are mostly doing nothing. The load is tasks stuck waiting for storage. So load average is not CPU percentage, and the same number can describe opposite problems. Compare load with nproc, look at the trend across the three averages, and then read the CPU line to see what kind of load it is. reportd's host looks like host B. Next: memory, and why low free memory is usually fine.

The second suspect is memory, and the most common mistake is reading free memory as the measure of health. Chapter eight showed why it isn't. Linux deliberately fills spare RAM with cache, and gives it back the moment programs need it. A healthy busy server often has very little free memory. Pressure shows up as behaviour instead, and the card gathers three kinds of evidence. vmstat, sampled every five seconds, has swap columns. si and so are pages swapped in and swapped out per second. Occasional swapping is normal. Sustained swapping in both directions, as here, means the system keeps evicting memory it needs again soon after, which is called thrashing. The second source is pressure stall information, in slash proc slash pressure slash memory. It reports the share of recent time that some tasks, or all tasks, were stalled waiting for memory. Thirty-one percent over the last ten seconds is a lot of lost work. The third is the kernel log. When reclaim can't free enough, the out-of-memory killer picks a process and ends it, and logs which one and how much memory it held. Here it killed reportd, and the message begins with memory cgroup, a detail section eight will explain. The table summarises the signals worth trusting. So, free memory is not memory pressure. Judge memory by stalls, swapping and the OOM log. Next: storage, and the difference between busy and slow.

The third suspect is storage, and here the trap is the word busy. A disk can be busy without being slow, and it can be slow while moving very little data. iostat dash x, from the sysstat package, separates four quantities, and the scene labels each. Throughput is how much data moves, in kilobytes per second. Latency is how long each request takes, in milliseconds: r await for reads and w await for writes. The queue, a q u dash s z, is the average number of requests waiting. And percent util is the share of time the device had at least one request in progress. Now read this device. Reads take zero point four milliseconds, which is fine. Writes take thirty-nine milliseconds, nearly a hundred times longer, with an average of thirty-five requests queued. Something is writing in bulk, and every write queues behind it. What users feel is latency, and reportd's requests are stuck behind that queue, which is also why host B's tasks were in state D. Notice the last column: ninety-nine point eight percent utilisation. On an old single spinning disk, that would mean saturated. An NVMe drive handles many requests in parallel, so one hundred percent util only says there was always something in flight, not that it couldn't take more. On solid-state storage, await and the queue are the better evidence. So the disk hypothesis is gaining support. But what is doing all the writing? Hold that question. Next: the network's view of the same incident.

From the clients' side, this incident looks like a network problem: timeouts and five oh three errors. The server's own evidence tells a more precise story. For a listening socket, ss shows two queue numbers that mean something special. Recv Q is the number of connections that have completed the TCP handshake but haven't yet been accepted by the application, and Send Q is the limit of that queue. reportd's listener shows one hundred and twenty-nine waiting against a limit of one hundred and twenty-eight. The queue is full. nstat reads the kernel's network counters, and listen overflows shows over four thousand connections dropped because that queue had no room. Retransmissions, by contrast, are low, so packets aren't being lost on the path. The table turns that into a rule of thumb. A full accept queue points at the application accepting too slowly. Rising retransmissions point at loss somewhere on the path or a congested link. Errors and drops on the interface point at this host's network card or driver. And traffic at the link's full speed points at bandwidth itself. Here, the network is carrying everything it's given. The queue is filling behind reportd, because reportd is slow to accept, because, as the previous sections suggested, its threads are waiting on storage. A network symptom with an application cause is extremely common, and the habit of following the queue to whoever isn't draining it is what finds it. Next: putting all of the evidence on one timeline.

Each tool so far has shown one layer. The next step is to put everything on a single timeline, because the order in which things changed is often the strongest evidence you have. The table merges four sources for Tuesday. apt's history log records every package transaction, and at one forty, reportd was upgraded from two point four to two point five. At two, the journal shows the nightly report starting, as it always does. From two until nine thirty, iostat shows write latency rising from one millisecond to thirty-nine. At nine, the access log shows user latency at eight seconds and five oh threes beginning. And at nine thirty, the journal shows the report finally finishing. It normally takes twenty minutes; this time it took seven and a half hours. The card shows the commands that built it: apt's history log for changes, and journalctl with since and until for each unit's view of the same window. It's very tempting to stop here and declare the upgrade guilty. But the plan's caution belongs exactly at this point. A correlation is not a cause. The upgrade and the long report both start around two, so which one is responsible? Perhaps the new version's report writes differently. Perhaps the report was always going to be slow on Tuesdays and the upgrade is a coincidence. Or a third thing explains both. A genuine cause predicts something you haven't observed yet. If the new report is the cause, then watching it should show what it is doing to the disk. That's the next section: watching the report's system calls.

When metrics say something is wrong but not why, you can watch a process directly. strace shows each system call it makes, every request to the kernel, with its arguments, its result and, with dash capital T, how long it took. Here it is attached to the running nightly report, process fifty-one twenty, showing only two kinds of call: opening files and fsync. The first two lines show the report trying to open store twelve's CSV and getting ENOENT, no such file, twice. That's chapter two's error, now reported by name, and it's a separate bug worth noting. The third line is an EACCES, permission denied, on an archive index, chapter four's error. And the fourth line is the answer to our question. A single fsync took two point eight seven seconds. The summary mode, dash c, totals time per system call, and it shows that the new report calls fsync after every row it writes. Chapter eight explained what fsync costs: each call waits until data reaches stable storage. Thousands of them, one after another, produce exactly the deep write queue iostat showed. The prediction from the previous section is confirmed. Now the plan's cautions, which are not optional. strace needs permission to trace the process, normally root. It slows the traced process considerably, so on a struggling production service, it can make things worse. And it prints real data: file contents, paths, sometimes passwords or tokens, which then sit in your terminal and logs. Trace narrowly, briefly, and then detach. Next: why reportd was killed when the host had memory to spare.

Section three found the OOM killer ending reportd, but the host had memory to spare. This section explains that apparent contradiction, and with it, what containers really are. free shows the host with twelve gigabytes available. But every systemd unit runs in its own control group, or cgroup, a kernel feature that groups processes so their resources can be counted and limited together. Chapter six gave reportd a MemoryMax of two hundred and fifty-six megabytes, and that setting is simply the memory dot max file in reportd's cgroup directory under slash sys slash fs slash cgroup. memory dot current shows it right at that ceiling, and memory dot events shows the kernel's OOM killer has acted inside this group three times. The journal confirms it in systemd's words: failed with result oom-kill. The host had memory. reportd's group did not. During the slow report, requests piled up inside reportd faster than it could finish them, and its memory grew until it hit the limit. The limit did its job: it protected the rest of the machine from reportd. A second kernel feature, namespaces, answers a different question: not how much a process may use, but what it can see. Separate namespaces give a process its own view of process IDs, mounts, network interfaces and users. A container is simply processes combining both features. That has two consequences worth remembering. Inside a container, tools like top may still report the host's totals, not the container's limits. And containers are not complete isolation, because every container on a host shares one kernel. Last in this chapter: fixing it, and proving the fix.

The evidence points at the new report calling fsync after every row. The fix is also a hypothesis, and it gets tested the same way. The plan at the top has four parts. Make one change only: here, a configuration setting that commits every thousand rows instead of every row. If you change three things at once and the problem goes away, you won't know which one mattered, or what the other two broke. Measure it the same way as before: replay Tuesday's report on the same host, under the same load, so before and after are comparable. Keep the rollback ready: the previous configuration file is saved, and going back is one restart. And record what you did. The table shows the result. The report now takes nineteen minutes instead of seven and a half hours. Write latency during the report falls from thirty-nine milliseconds to two. And the number users actually feel, the ninety-fifth percentile response time, falls from eight seconds back to under half a second, close to last week's baseline. The last row is the trade-off, and it belongs in the table, not in a footnote. Committing every thousand rows means a power cut in the middle of the report could lose up to a thousand rows instead of one. That's acceptable here, because chapter five made the report idempotent: rerunning it rebuilds the missing rows. For a payments system, the answer might be different. Every performance gain has a cost somewhere. Diagnosis is complete when you can state the cause, the evidence and the cost. Next chapter: security, recovery and operating the whole system.

The final chapter brings everything together around operating reportd safely, and it starts with security as a set of specific questions. Not is the system secure, but: what could go wrong, how would it reach us, and what stops it? The table is a small threat model for reportd's host. A stolen SSH key arrives through port twenty-two and an account with sudo, so the controls are key-only logins, few people with sudo, and logs that show who did what. A bug in reportd is reached through the proxy, so reportd runs as its own user, in a sandbox, bound to loopback, which are chapters four, six and seven. A malicious package arrives through a repository, so the host uses Debian's sources only. And an operator mistake, perhaps the most likely of all, happens in a root shell, which is why sudo runs one command at a time, and why backups exist. Then measure the attack surface rather than guessing it. ss lists every listening socket: here reportd on loopback, SSH, and the proxy, and nothing else. The sudo group says exactly who can become root. find lists set-user-ID programs, which run with their owner's privileges; a new one appearing deserves a question. And every one of the six hundred and twelve installed packages is code you trust. Three principles follow. Every part of the system has a named owner who answers for it. Every identity gets only what its job needs. And whatever isn't used should be removed, because what isn't there can't be attacked. Next: patching, and changing access without locking yourself out.

Most real intrusions don't use clever new attacks. They use known flaws that were fixed months ago on systems that weren't updated. So patching is the cheapest and most effective control in this chapter. Debian's unattended-upgrades package installs security updates automatically every day, and a dry run shows what it would do. One subtlety: replacing a library on disk doesn't change programs that already loaded the old one. Until they restart, they keep running the vulnerable code, and needrestart lists which ones. Next, SSH, the front door from the threat model. The configuration goes in a drop-in file, in the same spirit as chapter six's unit drop-ins, so package upgrades never overwrite it. It turns off password logins, so only keys work. It refuses direct root logins, so every administrator arrives as themselves and uses sudo. And it limits logins to named groups. Each line closes a specific path. The plan's illustration is about how you apply a change like this, because a mistake in SSH configuration can lock you out of the machine you're fixing. The numbered steps are the safe sequence. Keep your current session, A, open throughout. Run sshd dash t to check the syntax. Reload rather than restart, so existing sessions survive. Then log in from a second session, B. If that works, close A. If it doesn't, you still have A to undo the change. And know in advance how to reach the console if everything else fails. The same sequence applies to firewall changes from chapter seven. Next: when correct permissions still aren't enough.

This section is the plan's worked illustration of evidence across layers. After an update to version two point six, reportd won't start. The journal gives the first fact: it can't open its TLS private key, permission denied. Chapter four's habits come first. Is it running as the identity we expect? sudo dash u reportd id says yes: user reportd, group reportd. Can that identity reach the file? namei dash l shows the key is readable by the reportd group, and every parent can be searched. By the classic rules, this access should succeed. So the refusal must come from a different check, and the kernel log has it: an AppArmor line, denied, operation open, profile reportd, and the exact path. The new version reads its key from a directory its AppArmor profile didn't allow. The fix is a profile change, not a chmod, and chmodding the key wider would have weakened security without fixing anything. The middle row names the independent checks. Ordinary permissions come first. Capabilities split root's power into single privileges, so a service can, for example, be given only the ability to bind to port four four three, instead of running as root. And mandatory access control is a policy loaded into the kernel that even root cannot override. Which one you meet depends on the distribution, and the table labels it. Debian and Ubuntu use AppArmor, with rules written as file paths. Fedora and Red Hat use SELinux, with rules written in terms of labels. The method is the same: read the denial, then change the policy deliberately. Next: secrets, and the evidence trail.

reportd now needs a database password, and the question is where to put it. The table follows the password to every place it would be readable. Put it in an Environment line in the unit file, and it's shown by systemctl show, and readable in slash proc slash pid slash environ by the service's owner and root. Pass it on the command line, and ps shows it to every user on the machine. Put it in an ordinary file with the default mode six four four, and anyone on the host can read it. The better option is systemd's credentials mechanism. The password lives in a file that only root can read. LoadCredential tells systemd to hand a copy to reportd when it starts, in a private directory that only that service can see, and reportd reads it from there at run time. Nothing else on the system ever has it. The other half of this section is evidence. When something goes wrong, whether a mistake or an attack, logs are how you reconstruct what happened, so they need protecting too. On Debian, only members of the adm and systemd-journal groups can read the full system journal, and that list should stay short. More importantly, an attacker who becomes root can edit or delete local logs. Shipping logs to a separate log server, as they're written, keeps a copy that the compromised host cannot change. And keep them long enough. Incidents are often discovered weeks after they began, and the logs from the first day are the ones you'll want. Next: proving that backups can actually be restored.

Chapter eight said a backup you haven't restored from is a hope, not a plan. Two numbers turn it into a plan you can test. The recovery point objective is how much recent data you can afford to lose. reportd takes nightly backups, so up to twenty-four hours of records could be lost; if that's too much, back up more often. The recovery time objective is how long the service can be down. Here, two hours. These are business decisions, so agree them with the people who rely on reportd, not just among administrators. Then prove them with a drill. The table is the plan's supplied restore evidence, from a quarterly drill on a scratch host, never on top of production. The order matters. First the dependencies: a host, with the right version of reportd installed. Then the data: the state database, copied back, with a checksum that matches the one recorded when the backup was taken. Then the database's own integrity check. Then the reports archive, with its file count. And finally the application: a real request to slash reports slash latest that returns the right totals. The total time, thirty-one minutes, is your measured recovery time, comfortably inside the objective. The card shows the most important principle. Validate the data, not just the files. A file can copy perfectly and still contain a broken database. So the drill runs SQLite's integrity check, and compares a row count with the count the backup job recorded. Only then is the backup known to be good. Next: recovering each layer, and two very different incidents.

When something breaks, the first job is to recover, and the table collects the recovery paths you have already learned, one per layer. If the system won't boot, chapter six's older kernel or rescue target gets you a working shell. If a service fails, its status and journal identify the problem, and the fastest recovery is often to roll back the package or configuration that changed. If the network is broken, often by your own change, the console from chapter seven lets you revert it. And if storage fails, chapter eight's sequence applies: stop writing, copy, then restore. The plan's contrast is in the second table, because two incidents that both feel like emergencies need opposite instincts. Suppose an SSH key has been stolen. The first move is containment: remove the key and end its sessions, before anything else. Then investigate what it touched, using the auth log and the journal. And until you know, don't trust the host; it may need rebuilding from scratch. Now suppose the reports were deleted by mistake. Nothing hostile happened, the host is fine, and the first move is simply to stop writes and restore from the last good backup, validated as in the previous section. Restoring first after a compromise can bring the attacker's changes back. Investigating at length before restoring lost data just extends the outage. The card shows a service rollback concretely. One honest caveat: pinning the old version requires a repository that still has it, here reportd's own, and apt-mark hold prevents the next upgrade from undoing the rollback. Next: making changes, and talking during incidents.

Look back at this course's incidents and most of them began with a change: an upgrade, a configuration edit, a new firewall rule. So the last operational habit is making changes deliberately. The first card is a change record, written before the reportd two point six upgrade. What is changing, and why. The risk: the service might fail to start, which staging already showed, in section three. How it will be tested. The rollback, and how long it takes: under five minutes. And the window, announced to the people who use reportd. Writing it takes ten minutes, and it forces you to know the rollback before you need it. The second card is a runbook for reportd being down. It's written before the incident, by someone calm, and used during it, by someone who may not be. Each step is an ordered check pointing at evidence from an earlier chapter: which class of failure curl reports, the service's status and journal, disk space and inodes, the cgroup's OOM count, recent changes. And step six is a time limit: if it's still down after fifteen minutes, roll back the last change first and investigate afterwards. Restoring service usually matters more than understanding the cause immediately. Finally, communication. People affected by an outage need four things in every update: the impact, who is affected and how; what is known, with times; what is not known yet, said plainly; and when the next update will come. Then keep to that time, even if there's nothing new. And afterwards, hold a blameless review: not who made the mistake, but what made it easy to make, and what will make it harder next time. Last: the whole system, in one picture.

In chapter one, reportd was an empty directory and a first command. Here it is now, as one picture. Its files live in the places chapter two described. It runs as its own identity, from chapter four. A unit and a timer, from chapter six, start it, supervise it and run its nightly report. It listens on loopback behind TLS, from chapter seven. Its data sits on a logical volume, from chapter eight. Its logs go to the journal and are rotated. Its memory and access are limited by its cgroup and sandbox, from chapters six and nine. And it has a recovery plan: tested backups, a drill and a runbook, from chapters eight and ten. Every card names the chapter that built it, and every one is something you can now explain. The table is the skill this course has really been building. When a symptom crosses layers, the goal isn't to guess the final answer immediately, but to name the next piece of evidence. Five oh threes from the proxy point to reportd's accept queue and journal, a network symptom with an application cause. Writes failing on a disk with free space point to inodes, or a deleted-but-open file. A start failure after an update points to the journal, then permissions, then policy. An OOM kill on a host with free memory points to the cgroup's limit. One honest boundary to finish with. This course has given you working models of a Linux system. Real operational competence comes from practice on real systems, ideally with someone experienced alongside. From here, you might go deeper into one distribution, into networking, into security, or into the kernel and container platforms.
